text: On the Fourth of July, when Mother, Nellie, and the children came down for a week, the company tired me out, though Jennie saw to everything. <break time="0.8s" /> John says that if I do not pick up faster, he shall send me to Weir Mitchell in the fall, but I do not want to go there at all. <break time="0.8s" /> I cry at nothing, and cry most of the time, though of course I never do when John is here, or anybody else, but only when I am alone. <break time="0.8s" /> Lying on this great immovable bed, which is nailed down, I believe, I follow that pattern about by the hour, determined to reach some sort of conclusion. <break time="0.8s" /> In a certain light there is a sub pattern behind the outside one, a strange, provoking, formless sort of figure that seems to skulk behind that silly front design. <break time="0.8s" /> The faint figure behind grows clearer every day, and the longer I watch it, the more it looks like a woman stooping down and creeping about behind that pattern. <break time="0.8s" /> One moonlit night I told John that I was not gaining here and wished he would take me away, but he said our lease would be up in only three weeks. <break time="0.8s" /> Bless her little heart, he said, she shall be as sick as she pleases, and then he begged me never to let that false and foolish fancy enter my mind. <break time="0.8s" /> So I said no more about it, but I lay awake for hours, trying to decide whether the front pattern and the back pattern really moved together.
